cues.text: In 1412, Father Lazzaro da Verona was prior of the Camaldolese abbey of Santa Maria in Bagno di Romagna, in Italy.
While celebrating Mass, he found himself assailed by sudden doubt about the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist he was about to consecrate.
Immediately after he pronounced the words of consecration over the wine, it transformed before him into what the earliest chronicler described as living Blood.
That chronicler was the historian Fortunio, who wrote that it began to seethe and rise until overflowing the chalice and falling onto the corporal spread beneath it.
Profoundly shaken, Father Lazzaro confessed his doubt openly to the faithful gathered for the Mass, along with the extraordinary sign that had answered it.

He was later transferred to Bologna to serve as chaplain to a Camaldolese convent, where he died in 1416, only a few years after the event that would keep his name attached to Bagno di Romagna for centuries afterward.
The stained corporal — venerated ever since as the relic of the 'Holy Cloth Soaked by Blood' — remained in the Camaldolese monks' care until the community's suppression in 1808.
It eventually passed to the Diocese of Cesena in 1975.

In 1958, a chemical analysis conducted at the University of Florence confirmed that the centuries-old stains on the cloth were indeed of hematic — blood — origin, a finding that has only deepened the devotion surrounding the relic.

The corporal remains on display in a dedicated chapel of the Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta at Bagno di Romagna, exposed each Sunday from March to November and carried in procession every year on the Feast of Corpus Christi.
Five centuries and more after a single monk's private crisis of faith, the cloth he left stained still draws the same question that first confronted him.
It asks what a believer does with doubt when it arrives not as an abstraction but at the altar itself.
